summary: Clarifies behavior of RTP endpoints that use multiple SSRCs, such as sending several streams in one session, with a focus on RTCP, and updates RFC 3550.

plainLanguage.summary: When one sender sends several streams in one call, this explains how to keep the quality reports tidy.

questions: multiple rtp streams in one session
what is an ssrc in rtp
how does rtcp work with multiple ssrcs
what is the rtp ssrc timeout rule
subtitle: How RTP endpoints that send several streams in one session should behave, especially when sending RTCP reports.

tldr.problem: RTP was written assuming each endpoint has one SSRC, but endpoints now send several streams in one session, and the original rules for RTCP reporting, aggregation and timeouts were unclear for that case.
tldr.mechanism: Every SSRC is treated as a separate participant. Their RTCP reports may be aggregated into compound packets under adjusted size and scheduling rules, feedback SSRC choice is clarified, and one uniform SSRC timeout rule of 5*Td is set.
tldr.outcome: The RFC updates RFC 3550 and RFC 4585 so that multi-stream endpoints report and time out SSRCs consistently.

today: RFC 8108 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2017. It updates RFC 3550 and RFC 4585, and the unit metadata shows nothing that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Endpoints Send Multiple Streams
sections.content:
Early RTP assumed one media source, one RTP stream and one SSRC per endpoint per session, with separate sessions for each media type. The specification was not consistently written for anything else, so it is unclear in places.

The RFC lists four use cases:

  • Endpoints with several capture devices, such as telepresence rooms with multiple cameras or microphones.
  • Several media types, such as audio and video, in a single RTP session to reduce transport flows.
  • Central devices that generate several streams, including mixers and the selective forwarding middlebox described in RFC 7667.
  • Several SSRCs for one media source, for example a retransmission stream per RFC 4588 or the layers of scalable video coding.
sections.plainLanguage: One person can have many cameras, send both sound and picture, or send a main stream plus a repair copy. All of them travel in the same call.

sections.title: RTP and Bandwidth With Many SSRCs
sections.content:
RTP is inherently a group protocol. Unless signaling restricts it, an endpoint can expect data from many SSRCs in one session, whether the transport is point to point or multicast, because the session is defined by its shared SSRC space and not by the transport connections. Mixers can also make some SSRCs visible only in the contributing source (CSRC) list.

Each endpoint has an allocated share of the session bandwidth. It does not have to divide that share evenly among its streams. It may shift bandwidth between SSRCs, or enable and disable streams, provided its total sending rate stays within its share.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone in a call gets a fixed amount of internet. You may give your main camera more of yours, as long as the total stays the same.

sections.title: RTCP Reporting With Multiple SSRCs
sections.content:
The core rule is that implementations MUST treat each SSRC as a separate participant. Each SSRC keeps its own RTCP state and interval, and without the optimisation in the Work in Progress draft cited as [MULTI-STREAM-OPT], each SSRC reports on every other one, including those on the same endpoint.

On joining a unicast session, an endpoint MUST NOT send more than four compound RTCP packets with zero initial delay, regardless of SSRC count. This matches the TCP maximum initial window of four packets from RFC 3390. Those packets MAY aggregate reports from several SSRCs, and senders should be prioritised. Remaining reports follow the normal timing rules.

Reports from several SSRCs may be aggregated into one compound packet if it begins with an SR or RR, avg_rtcp_size is maintained correctly, and scheduling follows the new rules. For each reporting SSRC, avg_rtcp_size is updated with div_packet_size, the packet size divided by the number of SSRCs reporting in it. Peers that skip this get an overly long interval and may time out aggregated SSRCs. If compatibility with non-updated endpoints matters, aggregation SHOULD be limited to two reports or not used.

For scheduling, each SSRC keeps its own timer tn. When one expires, and the packet is not an early RTCP packet, the endpoint SHOULD add reports from other SSRCs in order of increasing tn while they fit within the path MTU. Afterwards tp, tn and T_rr_last are updated for each SSRC included, using an average effective transmission time. Simulations cited in the RFC found no significant negative impact on scheduling.
sections.plainLanguage: Each stream counts as its own person writing reports. To save paper, one envelope may carry several reports, but the envelope size is split fairly so the counting stays honest.

sections.title: Feedback Packets and Early RTCP
sections.content:
With the RTP/AVPF and RTP/SAVPF profiles from RFC 4585, an endpoint with several SSRCs must choose which sends each feedback packet. Feedback about a media type SHOULD come from an SSRC that receives that type. Notifications or indications about data the endpoint processed MUST come from the SSRC used for that data. If separate SSRCs send and receive, the matching one SHOULD be used. Some messages need consistency, since a TMMBR limit must be removed by the same SSRC that set it.

To schedule early feedback, the RFC changes three things. An endpoint decides point-to-point versus multiparty by counting distinct CNAME values of the SSRCs it sees, and MUST NOT decide from unicast versus multicast or from the SSRC count. The check for an already scheduled feedback packet MUST consider all local SSRCs. And if an SSRC cannot send early, the feedback MAY be queued into any packet within its maximum useful lifetime, T_max_fb_delay.

The CNAME rule can misclassify some cases, such as a selective forwarding middlebox or an endpoint with several synchronization contexts. Reporting groups from the draft are the suggested fix.
sections.plainLanguage: When one person has many voices in a call, the right voice should speak up about the right thing, and the same voice should take back what it said earlier.

sections.title: Adding and Removing SSRCs
sections.content:
An endpoint always needs at least one SSRC for RTCP, even if it sends no media. Others learn about SSRCs from RTP and RTCP packets or from non-RTP signaling. If an endpoint that has never sent wants to start, it is RECOMMENDED to reuse its existing SSRC, because extra SSRCs lengthen reporting intervals. A second stream needs a new SSRC, and an SSRC cannot change media type or clock rate, so a new stream often needs a new SSRC.

An SSRC leaves a session either by timing out or by an RTCP BYE packet, and sending BYE is RECOMMENDED. After a BYE, a restarted stream needs a new SSRC. A temporary pause should instead keep sending RTCP so the context stays in place. An endpoint that stops all streams but stays in the session MUST keep at least one SSRC for RTCP reporting and feedback.
sections.plainLanguage: Say goodbye properly when you leave for good, but if you only step out for a moment, keep your seat warm.

sections.title: Uneven Rates, SSRC Timeouts and Tuning
sections.content:
An RTP session has one set of RTCP parameters, so all sending SSRCs share a base reporting interval, and all receivers share another. This is awkward when streams differ widely, such as audio in tens of kilobits per second beside multi-megabit video. Using one session per media source avoids that, but combining them reduces port use and eases NAT and firewall traversal. More SSRCs also means more cross reporting.

The RTP/AVPF suppression mechanism (T_rr_interval) can stretch the gap between regular reports, up to 1.5*T_rr_interval + 1.5/1.21828*Td. Under RTP/AVPF with a non-zero T_rr_interval, a single lost RTCP packet could then time an SSRC out. To fix this, all SSRCs in a session MUST use the same timeout rule: for RTP/AVP, RTP/SAVP, RTP/AVPF and RTP/SAVPF the timeout interval SHALL be 5*Td, with Td calculated using a Tmin of 5 seconds. This changes the first paragraph of Section 3.5.4 of RFC 4585. Mixing the two profiles in one session is NOT RECOMMENDED, but if done with non-updated RTP/AVPF endpoints, T_rr_interval SHOULD be 4 seconds.

The RFC also covers tuning. With the AVP profiles, bandwidth settings and the scaled minimum interval are the levers. With AVPF, T_rr_interval gives extra control, and if Td is to be below T_rr_interval it is RECOMMENDED to be under 1/4 of it. There is no way to use different regular reporting intervals per media type except separate RTP sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone in the call must use the same rule for when to decide someone has left, otherwise people get kicked out just because their check-ins are a little slow.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: For SRTP (RFC 3711) and RTP/SAVPF (RFC 5124), the cryptographic context of a compound secure RTCP packet is the SSRC of the sender of the first RTCP sub-packet. That may matter for per-SSRC keying such as MIKEY. Otherwise the usual RTP security considerations apply, and sending several streams from one endpoint in one session does not appear to have different security consequences than spreading them over several sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: Locks work the same as before. The only detail is that a bundled report uses the key of whoever's report is first in the bundle.

items.title: Multiple capture devices
items.text: Several cameras or microphones of the same type send streams in one session.

items.title: Multiple media types
items.text: Audio and video share a single RTP session.

items.title: Stream mixers
items.text: Mixers and selective forwarding middleboxes generate many streams.

items.title: One source, many SSRCs
items.text: Retransmission or layered video use extra SSRCs.
